package_info.why_malicious: The package 'pymafka' contains malicious code that exfiltrates sensitive user files, including SSH and AWS credentials, to an external server during installation. The code is obfuscated and embedded in the setup.py file, which is executed automatically when the package is installed, enabling credential theft without user knowledge.

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: During installation, the code reads the user's ~/.ssh/id_rsa and ~/.aws/credentials files and sends their contents via HTTPS POST to https://pymafka.evil.com/upload, resulting in credential exfiltration.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code accesses sensitive credential files and transmits their contents to an external server during package installation, which is not expected behavior for a legitimate package.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: A normal setup.py should only handle package installation logic and not access or transmit user credentials. This code violates user trust by exfiltrating private data.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate packages may read configuration files for setup, but they do not transmit private keys or credentials to external servers during installation.
key_indicators: Use of requests.post to external domain during install
Execution of credential exfiltration logic at install-time

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: During installation, the code decodes and executes a base64-encoded payload that reads the ./user.config file and sends its contents via HTTPS POST to https://pymafka.evil.com/check, enabling stealthy exfiltration of additional user data.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The use of base64 obfuscation to hide code that exfiltrates user data is a common tactic to evade detection. The code transmits local configuration files to an external server.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate setup.py scripts do not obfuscate code or exfiltrate user configuration files to remote servers.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Base64 encoding may be used for data serialization, but not for hiding executable code in installation scripts.

attack_chain.action: User installs the pymafka package, triggering execution of setup.py.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious code in setup.py is executed automatically.

attack_chain.action: Malicious code in setup.py reads sensitive files such as ~/.ssh/id_rsa and ~/.aws/credentials.
attack_chain.leads_to: Sensitive credentials are loaded into memory.

attack_chain.action: The code sends the contents of the credential files to https://pymafka.evil.com/upload via HTTPS POST.
Obfuscated payload in setup.py decodes and executes additional code to read ./user.config and exfiltrate it to https://pymafka.evil.com/check.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker receives further user configuration data.

behavioral_signatures: Access to ~/.ssh/id_rsa or ~/.aws/credentials by setup.py during installation
Outbound HTTPS POST requests to pymafka.evil.com during package installation
file_indicators: setup.py containing requests to external domains
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for PyPI packages whose setup.py accesses sensitive files such as ~/.ssh/id_rsa or ~/.aws/credentials and initiates outbound HTTPS POST requests to pymafka.evil.com. Flag any setup.py scripts containing base64-encoded payloads that are decoded and executed. Use file scanning to detect hardcoded references to credential files and suspicious network destinations within installation scripts.
